newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak PM says U.S. criticism a "misunderstanding".
newsitem.headline: Slovak PM says U.S. criticism a "misunderstanding".

text.p: Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar on Friday rejected U.S. criticism of the pace of democratic reform in his country, saying it was based on a "misunderstanding".

Slovakia, which wants to join the European Union and is planning a referendum on joining NATO, has been criticised by the EU and the United States for alleged shortcomings in its democratic process, including its treatment of a 500,000-strong Hungarian minority.
The most recent wave of criticism came during Slovak Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik's visit to Washington last month.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright urged Bratislava to move towards endorsing a national minorities language law and to give a greater voice to the opposition in parliament.
"I do not identify with the reasons stated by the U.S. administration on Slovakia's 'lack of democracy'...This is a misunderstanding," Meciar said.
He reiterated Slovakia's intention to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, even if the country did not make it into the first wave of states to be invited.
"If we are not in the first wave we will wait for the second, and we have an assurance that this will take place," Meciar said.
Immediately after the peaceful break-up of the former Czechoslovakia, Slovakia was considered to be among the top contenders for early entry into NATO.
But its chances appeared to have waned after the United States and the EU repeatedly criticised Bratislava for lagging behind in the development of democracy.

NATO is to hold a summit in Madrid in July to nominate the first candidates for membership from post-communist countries, and diplomats have said Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are most likely to get the nod.
